rail_guard.text: Bath Spa. Our station is by Brunel. Our delays are timeless.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited. Where to?

then.text: Rain! The Romans built a whole bath here to get wet on purpose. I am living the dream.
Frost! Under this tunic I'm wearing two vests and a thermal. Very authentic. Don't tell the Emperor.
Torches lit by the Great Bath at dusk. The steam comes off the water like a ghost having a nice time.

roman_actor.text: Salve! I am Gaius Maximus, legionary. Er, volunteer. The cloak is itchy but I'm told it's authentic.
The Romans called this place Aquae Sulis, the waters of Sulis. Sulis was a Celtic goddess the Romans blended with Minerva. Smart marketing.

bath_buns.text: A Sally Lunn bun! Big, round, brioche-y. Sally Lunn herself is said to have baked them here in the 1680s.
You split them and fill them with cream or cheese. I was told never to say 'a dollop' about a thing this elegant.

abbey_verger.text: Bath Abbey has 52 windows, so many that it's called the Lantern of the West.
Look at the carved ladders on the front. Bishop Oliver King dreamed of angels climbing them. Health and safety was not consulted.

then.text: Rain! Very Austen. Someone always gets caught in a shower and falls in love. I'm just getting damp.
A fine day for a stroll along the Royal Crescent. Bonnets optional, but encouraged.

austen_fan.text: Jane Austen lived here from 1801 to 1806 and, honestly, disliked it. Then she wrote about it for the rest of her life.
Northanger Abbey and Persuasion are both partly set in Bath. The Assembly Rooms are still lovely for the stroll and the eye contact.

then.text: Rain makes the acoustics even better under the arches. It also makes the coins slippery.
Sun's out, crowd's out. I've played the same three tunes eleven times and nobody's noticed.

bridge_busker.text: {greeting} Do you take requests? I take coins. They don't wear the strings out as quickly.
I busk by the bridge because the acoustics are marvellous. Also the fudge shop is next door.

then.text: Fog over the Crescent. Now you truly can't tell the houses apart. I nearly went home to the neighbours'.
Frost on the lawn in front of the Crescent. It looks like icing on a very long cake.

crescent_resident.text: The Royal Crescent is Grade I listed. We may paint the front doors any colour, as long as it's white.
I've never counted the houses. They're all identical. You'd get lost trying.

boat_hirer.text: The Avon here is only knee-deep at the weir. Don't ask how I know.
Pulteney Weir is a horseshoe. Every year a duck goes over it on purpose. The duck has better balance than me.

then.text: We've pulled the Heritage Water. I'm selling lemonade now. It has no heritage whatsoever. Very refreshing.

else.text: Heritage Water! Straight from the mythical spring of Sulis herself! Four pounds a bottle, or three for ten, which is a worse deal.
Every bottle comes with a certificate. And a lanyard. The lanyard is the product, between you and me.

then.text: Well, it comes from a pipe. The pipe comes from the spring. The spring is the one in the Baths. Hot, green and mineral-y.
The Enclosure leased the overflow. 'Overflow' is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
You jot it down. The bottle is stamped: 'Sulis Minerva Heritage Water (tm). Do not drink. Do not return.'

else.text: Your loss. It's mostly minerals. And, er, heritage.

bath_astronomer.text: William Herschel found the planet Uranus from his back garden here in Bath, in 1781, with a telescope he built himself.
Clear night? Look up. Same stars Herschel saw, just fewer horses clattering past.
His sister Caroline found comets too. Bath's been a starry sort of city for a long time.
